runs.text: Made by Arshad · 28-fund review
Where each of the 28 funds stands

Nine funds are heavily exposed to an AI-led sell-off, but AI is not the only threat. Oil lurching on every Iran headline (Brent about $92.6 on 20 Nov, down from $115 in late October), a yen at almost 160 per dollar, the level that has triggered intervention, a 10-year US yield near 5% (about 4.9% on 20 Nov) with a December Fed hike close to certain, and rising tension around Taiwan each hit different funds. Combining all of these, 11 funds rate High or Very high overall risk. Only the money market funds and cash are close to safe in every scenario.
Why these 28:

together they form a comprehensive set covering cash in three currencies, government and corporate bonds, developed and emerging-market shares, real estate, commodities, gold and absolute return, across the US, Europe, the UK, Japan, Asia and the Pacific. Almost any market event shows up somewhere in the list.

Update · Sun 22 Nov 2026, 6 am Manila (covers the weekend and the week ahead)
Iran steps up attacks on Hormuz tankers and Bahrain as markets head into a short Thanksgiving week

Markets were shut for the weekend, but the Iran war heated up. On Saturday two tankers leaving the Strait of Hormuz were hit by projectiles off Oman, Iran said another tanker hit a mine and caught fire, and Bahrain intercepted Iranian air attacks. No injuries were reported. Qatari mediators visited Tehran on Friday, but neither side signalled a deal. Oil ended last week lower, with Brent at $92.57. Over the week the S&P 500 fell 8.6% and the Nasdaq 10%, while bond yields dropped. This short US week brings inflation and growth data on Wednesday night, Manila time, and Wall Street is shut for Thanksgiving on Thursday. No fund rating changed.

cells.text: What happened
Funds affected
What it means
Iran stepped up attacks on shipping.

The UK maritime agency UKMTO said two tankers were struck by projectiles early on Saturday 21 Nov while leaving the strait near Khasab, Oman, with no casualties; Iran's navy said a separate tanker hit a mine east of the strait and caught fire (AP via ABC News, Al Jazeera via Yahoo). UKMTO counted about 19 vessels targeted in the first 18 days of November (Gulf News), and traffic through the strait is about 65% below pre-war levels (Investing.com). On Saturday evening Bahrain intercepted Iranian air attacks; a fire broke out at an industrial site, with no injuries (Gulf News).

Oil has largely shrugged off attacks this month, but Monday's open will show whether that holds. A jump in oil would lift the commodity fund (12) and the UK fund's energy shares (8), and hurt oil-importing Asia and Japan (22, 23, 27).
Diplomacy is stuck.

A Qatari delegation held two hours of talks in Tehran on Friday evening. Iran's deputy foreign minister said nuclear talks have not started, enriched material will not leave Iran, and the US blockade, now 130 days old according to US Central Command, is an act of war (Gulf News, AP via ABC News). In a Fox News interview on Saturday Trump said he wants a permanent deal that stops an Iranian bomb, but complained that Iran breaks deals (Investing.com).
With no deal in sight, the oil risk stays two-way: a breakthrough could send oil sharply lower, while a longer closure keeps inflation and rate-hike pressure high for the bond funds (28, 9).
Last week in numbers.

In the week to 20 Nov the S&P 500 fell 8.6%, the Nasdaq 10.0% and the Dow 8.0%; technology shares lost 12.5% and consumer staples only 2.1% (The Closing Print). The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.92% from 5.15% and the 2-year to 4.63% from 4.88%, and gold futures fell about 9% on the week (The Closing Print). Brent settled at $92.57 and US crude at $83.98, each down about 4–5% on the week (Gulf News).

A heavy week for the equity funds (6, 3, 4, 19), worst for the AI-heavy ones (13, 22, 24). The bond funds (28, 26, 25, 9) gained as yields fell, the first real sign this autumn of bonds cushioning a stock sell-off. The gold-miners fund (1) had a very bad week.
Coming up (Manila):

Mon 23 Nov, 10:45 pm: US flash business surveys (PMIs). Tue 24 Nov, 11 pm: US consumer confidence. Wed 25 Nov, morning: Dell and Workday results. Around 25 Nov: Bessent's deadline for answers from NVIDIA's board. Wed 25 Nov, 9:30 pm: US October inflation (PCE), third-quarter GDP, jobless claims and durable goods, all at once. Thu 26 Nov: US markets closed for Thanksgiving; Fri 27 Nov they close early, at 2 am Saturday Manila time (The Closing Print). OPEC+ meets on 29 Nov; the Fed decides on 8–9 Dec, US time.

Wednesday's inflation data matter most: a hot reading would cement a December Fed hike and pressure the bond funds (28, 9), while cash and money market funds (14) keep earning more. Dell and NVIDIA news steer the AI-heavy equity funds (6, 13, 22).

AI-crash scenario
Who gets hurt, who holds

In an AI-led crash I estimate the most AI-concentrated funds could fall 30–40%, broad developed-market equity funds 20–30%, and cash would hold its value. Government bonds would likely gain a few percent, but only if the crash lowers inflation fears rather than arriving with another oil shock.

My estimates from each fund's AI concentration, equity beta and volatility, calibrated to the 2000–02 dot-com bust (S&P 500 about −49%), 2022 (MSCI World −18%, US Treasuries −13%) and Korea's July 2026 chip crash (KOSPI −40% in six weeks). Not forecasts.
Scenario assumed.

AI capital spending is cut sharply, US mega-cap tech falls 40–50%, the S&P 500 falls 25–35% and Asian chip stocks repeat their July 2026 slide. The Fed responds by cutting rates. If inflation stays high instead (for example, the Strait of Hormuz closes again), the bond funds would not rise and only cash would hold.
Liquidity.
Every fund deals daily; settlement is typically 1–3 business days plus any platform processing time. In a crash the practical risks are:
Emerging-market and Asian equity funds (22, 24) and the commodity swap fund (12) can see prices gap and dealing spreads widen.
Funds can apply swing pricing or, in extreme cases, defer large redemptions; this matters most for the active and EM funds.
Selling after a fall locks in the loss. The 2000–02 and 2022 sell-offs both had sharp rebounds that punished late sellers.

Eight other risks in the news now, and which funds they hit

1 · Yen turmoil

The yen fell to about 163 per dollar in late July, prompting a joint US–Japan intervention (Japan reportedly spent around $85bn) that pushed it to 155. By mid-August most of that gain had reversed. It was near 158 on 27 Oct, and Finance Minister Katayama has warned she is ready to act again, with traders watching 160. In the week to 6 Nov the dollar traded between about 157.3 and 158.8 yen; hawkish Bank of Japan minutes and the stock rout helped the yen, but the strong US jobs report pushed the dollar back to the mid-158s. The pressures are a slow Bank of Japan (held at 1.25% on 30 Oct, though it signalled more hikes), PM Takaichi's 19 Oct signal that about ¥10 trillion of tax cuts may be funded with deficit bonds (debt is 204% of GDP), 10-year JGB yields near 3%, and an oil import bill that has only just started to ease (Brent near $98 on 6 Nov, from $115 in late October). On 12–13 Nov the dollar reached about 159.8–159.9 yen, the closest yet to 160. On 16 Nov it was near 159.6 after Japan reported that its economy shrank at a 0.1% annual rate in July–September. On 17 Nov it eased to about 159.2. On 18 Nov it held near 159.3, and on 19 Nov it was about 159.5 as the dollar index hit a 19-month high. The move can run either way: intervention or a carry-trade unwind could lift the yen 5% in days.

2 · Oil shock and the Strait of Hormuz

Brent settled at $115.32 on 28 Oct, about 75% higher than a year ago. On 10 Nov it briefly fell below $90 for the first time since August after Trump said the war was militarily effectively over. On 16 Nov Brent fell 3.6% to $92.44 even as Iran targeted Bahrain again, as the IEA forecast a surplus of about 1.7 million barrels a day this quarter. On 19 Nov Brent held near $92, close to a three-month low, amid reports that Trump is considering more strikes on Iran. On 20 Nov Brent settled at $92.57, about 4% lower on the week. On 21 Nov two tankers leaving the strait were hit by projectiles off Oman, Iran said another hit a mine and caught fire, and Bahrain intercepted Iranian air attacks; traffic through the strait is about 65% below pre-war levels, and Qatari mediation has produced no deal. Nothing is agreed, and the strait has been largely closed since March. This is a two-way risk. A deal could send oil sharply lower; Brent fell to about $72 during the brief June truce. A longer closure keeps inflation and rates high.

3 · Sticky inflation and rising bond yields

US CPI rose to 3.7% in September (core 2.6%). The Fed held on 28 Oct in a 10–2 vote, with both dissenters wanting a hike. The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.35%, the highest since 2002. On 10 Nov October CPI rose 0.4% in the month (core 0.3%), above forecasts; the 10-year yield jumped to about 5.01%, a December hike became close to fully priced, and Fed Governor Waller said a half-point move could be considered. On 18 Nov minutes of the October meeting showed nearly all officials expect a December hike, two floated half a point, and most worry inflation will persist; Waller said a quarter-point December move would need a signal of another in January. The 10-year yield eased to about 5.05–5.07% as oil fell. On 19 Nov Waller said the Fed needs either a half-point December hike or guidance for more; markets put about 90% odds on a quarter point, and the 10-year yield held near 5.05%. On 20 Nov investors fled stocks for bonds and the 10-year yield fell to about 4.91%, but Governor Cook warned against falling behind the curve, and hike odds stayed above 90%. Over the week to 20 Nov the 10-year yield fell to 4.92% from 5.15% and the 2-year to 4.63% from 4.88%; the October inflation (PCE) data are due on 25 Nov, US time. Rising yields hurt bonds, REITs and expensive growth stocks at the same time, as in 2022.

4 · French debt stress and a weaker euro

France's 10-year yield hit 4.98% on 21 Oct, a 24-year high, and its spread over Germany reached 157 bp, the widest since the euro crisis. EUR/USD fell 3.9% between 9 Sep and 23 Oct even though the ECB raised rates twice this year to 2.50%. Eurozone inflation is 3.8%, and the October PMI fell to a four-month low. On 29 Oct the ECB held, the euro touched a 17-month low, and Lagarde's early exit (7 Feb 2027, before the French election) was confirmed. On 18 Nov the euro fell to about $1.096, its lowest since April 2025. On 19 Nov it stayed near $1.096, and Germany's DAX fell about 1.1%.

5 · Taiwan tension and Asian currency stress

China held live-fire drills across five sea areas on 12–17 Oct, coast-guard ships harassed Taiwanese vessels on 18 Oct, and on 16 Oct Beijing drafted export curbs on about 40 technologies, including AI and chips. On 15 Oct foreign investors sold NT$165bn of Taiwan stocks in one day, Korean outflows for October passed $10bn, the Philippine peso passed 63 per dollar for the first time, and India and Indonesia intervened to support their currencies. On 16 Nov the US tightened rules on Chinese access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centres, and Taiwan's market fell about 6%. On 17 Nov Taiwan fell another 2.3% and Korea's KOSPI 2.6% to a six-month low. On 18 Nov the KOSPI rebounded about 1.9% to back above 5,000, and Taiwan edged up 0.1%, after NVIDIA's results. On 19 Nov Taiwan fell about 4.4% and the MSCI Asia-Pacific ex-Japan index hit a seven-month low, while Korea rose 1.4%. On 20 Nov Taiwan fell about 5.7% and Korea about 5.2%, putting Taiwan on course for its steepest weekly fall since October 1997.

6 · AI debt inside "safe" bond funds

AI-related borrowing has passed roughly $466–500bn this year and makes up about 10% of the largest long-term investment-grade bond ETFs. Oracle's 5-year CDS more than doubled to about 308 bp, Meta's and NVIDIA's hit records in October, and CoreWeave's implies a default probability above 60%. Pimco as a firm bought $18bn of Meta's Hyperion data-centre bond. On 28 Oct Alphabet reported that its long-term debt had jumped from $46.5bn to $125.1bn in a year, alongside $12.4bn of stock sales, to pay for AI. On 2 Nov Oracle filed to sell $10bn of stock and $10bn of senior notes for the same purpose. After the 3 Nov election, analysts flagged Democrats' openness to data-centre moratoriums, and on 4 Nov AI-infrastructure names fell (NVIDIA −3.2%, CoreWeave −9.9%, Vistra −13.8%) even as the market rallied. On 5 Nov the chip index fell 12.3% and the Nasdaq entered correction, as investors priced a slower, costlier AI build-out. On 11 Nov CoreWeave said it expects about $9bn of customer prepayments over three months and plans no more expensive debt through 2027; its shares jumped more than 20% and the chip index about 7%. On 19 Nov Anthropic raised a record $81.3bn in its IPO and its shares closed 17% above the $83 offer price, but CoreWeave swung from a 10.5% gain to a loss of about 5.5% as AI stocks slid again. On 20 Nov the AI sell-off deepened: NVIDIA fell 14%, AMD 13% and Anthropic 8.5%.

7 · UK Budget and gilts

The 10-year gilt yield touched 5.53% on 8 Oct, the highest since 2007. UK inflation is 3.5%, and markets expect a Bank of England hike on 5 Nov. The 28 Oct Budget kept about £15bn of fiscal headroom and gilts held steady, but it doubled the bank surcharge to 6%, a cost for the UK fund's banks. On 18 Nov UK inflation figures showed prices rising faster, and the 10-year gilt yield fell about 0.08 points to 5.29% as oil dropped.

8 · Gold's correction and Australia's rate hikes

Gold briefly fell below $4,000 on 23 Oct, about a quarter under its January record. It dropped alongside stocks as leveraged investors raised cash, so it did not behave as a safe haven that day. It slipped again on 29 Oct and fell 3.3% to a one-year low of $3,899 on 30 Oct as tech sold off, just above Standard Chartered's $3,886 warning level. It gained about 4.5% in the week to 6 Nov, its best week since August, ending near $4,050–4,080. On 12 Nov it fell about 2.9% to roughly $3,885 as the dollar firmed on Fed hike bets. On 18 Nov it fell about 3% to roughly $3,735–3,745, well below its 30 Oct low. On 19 Nov it fell about 2% to roughly $3,665 (futures), below $3,700 for the first time since September 2025. On 20 Nov it fell about 4.5% to roughly $3,519 (futures), its lowest since September 2025, heading for a weekly loss of about 8–9%. In Australia, the RBA has hiked four times this year to 4.60%, CPI is 4.0%, and Q3 core inflation of 3.7% beat forecasts on 28 Oct, and on 3 Nov the RBA hiked a fifth time to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, in a split 6–3 vote that dropped its tightening bias. On 19 Nov the Australian dollar hit a 10-month low after weak jobs data.

On 13 Nov chip stocks slid again (chip index about −3.4%, NVIDIA −2.0%) and the S&P 500 closed 0.4% lower at 7,561.67, but it still gained about 2.5% for the week, its first weekly gain in five; October producer prices were up 6.5% on a year, and the 10-year yield closed near 5.15% (Yahoo Finance, CappNotes). Over the weekend Iran said a supertanker sank after hitting a mine in the strait, and drone and missile attacks on Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were intercepted (AFP via RTÉ, Gulf News). On 16 Nov new US curbs on Chinese access to advanced chips sent the chip index down about 4.6% and the S&P 500 about 1.9% to roughly 7,415, more than 5% below its record, while Brent fell 3.6% to $92.44 on the IEA's surplus forecast (Reuters, Bloomberg). On 17 Nov stocks fell again before NVIDIA's results: the S&P 500 lost 1.2% to about 7,327, about 6.3% below its record, and Korea's KOSPI closed below 5,000 for the first time since February (Reuters, AP). On 18 Nov NVIDIA's revenue beat forecasts at $115.8bn, but its shares fell about 3%; the S&P 500 slipped about 0.3% for a fifth straight fall while the Dow lost about 1.2%, and US crude fell 3–4% and gold about 3% (Wealth Professional, Yahoo Finance, Bloomberg). On 19 Nov Anthropic's record $81.3bn IPO opened 34% above its $83 price and closed up 17%, but an early rally faded and the S&P 500 fell 2.0% to 7,175.83, a sixth straight loss and 8.2% below its record, while gold fell to a 14-month low (Yahoo Finance, AP). On 20 Nov the S&P 500 fell 3.7% to 6,910.39, a seventh straight loss, and closed in a correction about 11.6% below its record; the Nasdaq lost 5.3% and turned negative for 2026, NVIDIA fell 14%, and gold fell about 4.5% (Yahoo Finance, CBS News). In the week to 20 Nov the S&P 500 fell 8.6%, the Nasdaq 10.0% and the Dow 8.0%, while the 10-year yield fell to 4.92% (The Closing Print). On 21 Nov Iran stepped up attacks on tankers near Hormuz and on Bahrain (AP, Gulf News).

In an inflationary environment stocks and bonds can fall together, as in 2022. If an AI crash instead triggers a growth scare and Fed cuts, Treasuries and high-quality bonds should rally. Which of those two worlds arrives decides whether the bond funds protect you; only the cash-like funds are safe in both.

If the S&P 500 falls 5%, 10% or 20%: which funds to add

A guide to which of the 28 funds tend to be worth adding as a sell-off deepens, using the S&P 500's fall from its 7,819 record (6 Oct 2026) as the trigger, because it is the market's main gauge. The idea is to add the steadier, low-AI funds first and the high-growth, AI-heavy funds only once they are much cheaper. Purchases are funded mainly from cash and from bonds that have risen. Where we are now: at the close on Friday (20 Nov, US time) the S&P 500 was 6,910.39, about 11.6% below its record, so it has passed both the −5% level (~7,430), first crossed on 5 Nov, and the −10% level (~7,040), crossed on 20 Nov. The −20% level (~6,255) is about 9.5% lower.

In an AI or growth crash, Treasuries usually rise, so selling some bonds to buy stocks works. In an oil or inflation shock, bonds may fall too: fund purchases from cash (14) instead, and consider trimming the commodity fund (12), which is likely to have risen.

Returns

are total returns in the share-class currency, net of fees; 5-year figures are annualised. EUR, GBP and JPY classes are shown in those currencies, not USD. Most are to 30 September 2026; some to 31 August or earlier where that was the latest public figure.

the USD cash account rate, L&G Diversified EUR returns, the L&G Diversified USD 1-year return, and Vanguard Japan 1- and 5-year returns. The fund providers can supply them on request.
AI-crash estimates
are my judgement, not model output or forecasts.
Volatility 1–7
(shown as "Risk 1–7" in the earlier version) is my rating on the familiar SRI scale for how much each fund's price swings; it is not the official KID rating.
Other key risks
are non-AI threats backed by news from 4–26 October 2026: currencies, oil, inflation and rates, sovereign debt, geopolitics and credit. Each is rated Low, Medium or High for that fund.
Overall risk

combines AI exposure, those other risks and volatility into one judgement, on a scale from Very low to Very high, for an investor whose spending currency is the US dollar. Funds 11 and 15 carry a note because their risk is much lower in their own currency. These ratings are my judgement and will change with the news; the dates to watch are listed under Other risks.
